The debate on issuance policy and “MVS” continues on ethresearch. I recommend everyone to read the back and forth, with my latest response from today. Something that I wish to highlight is how to approach the “median yield” of a non-pooled staker. It is common to present this data in a way that can mislead solo stakers.

First of all, the expected yield is the most relevant measure to solo stakers and delegating stakers alike. This is the preferred measure, coupled with a measure of variability over a time frame of one or a few years. A prospective solo staker might also want to know what the median outcome or any other order statistics would be over some given time period, perhaps a year or two, or until their hardware investments have reached their depreciation horizon. Order statistics can thus be relevant on a per-validator basis over longer time.

The issue is that numerous webpages and researchers instead rely on things like the median across all validators over some minuscule time period, and then average these medians over time. This fails to capture the probabilistic outcome facing the solo staker. It is obfuscated by a skewed daily distribution combined with the law of large numbers. Half of the validators will never propose a block during the same day, yet half will still propose within a few months. The signal is destroyed by computing the median at the wrong point across the wrong dimension.

To check if it is raining, do not extend your hand and measure the median number of fingers impacted by raindrops every millisecond. The result will always be zero; yet it might still rain.

The presented figure is an idealized simulation of how the yearly distribution of yields varies with pool size under current rewards (refer to the link below for details). The tiny vertical line segment of the black curve is the small fraction of solo stakers that do not have a block proposal or sync-committee duty over a year. This is presented as the “all-time median” on sites such as Rated. I do not have anything in particular against this specific site, but their statistic was used by the authors of the MVS post to model the outcome for solo stakers, so I highlight it here.

The real median outcome facing solo stakers after one year is indicated by a black arrow. As evident, it comes fairly close already to the expected yield. After two years of solo staking with a single validator (blue curve), there are hardly any 32-ETH validators that have not had proposal or sync-committee duties, and so almost all are above the "median" baseline.

To conclude, going forward, we must make sure to not rely on an erroneous median for modeling purposes, and to communicate proper statistical distributions to solo stakers.

The link to the original MVS post is https://t.co/2jnHn6tdfA

My latest response is at https://t.co/EPnhpIJgEp

The context of the discussion is which measure of revenue to adhere by. The MVS post asserts that the short-term median computed across all validators and then averaged over time is an appropriate measure of revenue for solo stakers. I assert this to be incorrect. Since you were listed as having provided feedback on that post, I would like to understand if you think the short-term median is an appropriate measure for revenue, to then be inserted into an analytical framework?

Please clarify what you mean by "the rate at which a staker accumulates ETH".
name: Anders Elowsson 🌻

full_text:
i think it was your own interpretation that a short-term median is an appropriate measure of solo stakers. we opined that the average is a misleading number due to the extreme positive skew observed in EL rewards. 

If you design a system around the viability of solo stakers being dependent on winning low probability events, then that will naturally further discourage solo stakers, assuming they are purely economically driven. This is our main point of concern. 

While we see the median as a more relevant measure of central tendency for solo stakers and smaller node operators, we've also referred to the preliminary paper from a @cyberfund grantee that shows that solo stakers earn less than pools. So whether the focus is on mean or median, the key point is that the conclusion is the same: solo stakers are disadvantaged from a yield perspective with a higher % of fixed costs.

Finally a concern not addressed in our response is the platform risk that the issuance curve change imposes on a variety of downstream applications that have built economies and use cases around. Major DeFi protocols, including LSTs, borrow/lend platforms, and stablecoins, could be severely impacted by the EF's decision. I'd like to ask, are you fully aware of the downstream implications of these proposed changes?
name: Sonya Kim

full_text:
You specifically used a short-term median for modeling solo stakers' revenue: the one from Rated. This is how the MVS model came to set their APR to 2.4% (corresponding to the tiny vertical line segment in the figure). The positive skew can instead be captured using the per-validator distribution, as shown in the figure of my first tweet.

If we are to discuss the viability of solo staking, we must model their revenue correctly. 

My reading of that paper is a take-home of 97.8% for solo stakers, as I discussed in the comment.  I'd have to study it closer to draw conclusions; I already had several objections upon my first look. There is then noisy subgroup data that seems perilous to draw conclusions from. In general, I do not think it is appropriate to shift the discussion to another paper before sorting out the analysis of the MVS post. In any case, there is a stark difference here between comparing solo stakers and SSPs at 3.36% vs. 3.44% (97.8% of the revenue) and at 2.4% vs. 3.44%. 

I feel I have addressed the concerns. I would rather suggest that my point about the short-term median has been addressed head-on in a forthright manner. Searching "borrow", "lend" and "stablecoin" gives no hits on the ethresearch post. I believe you may have tweeted about it sometime in the past, but that is another matter. Perhaps you meant that this is a new concern that I should address now? 

I will try to address this in a tweet (though I would still prefer ethresearch). First of all, this is not an "EF decision", just to get that out of the way. Still, there is value in having neutral researchers work on a topic, as opposed to those funded with a specific outcome in mind.

The stated problem is that applications (have) come to depend on high issuance yield to sustain themselves, and it will be detrimental to them if that yield is removed. Or, as framed in your tweet, "built economies and use cases" around it. The way I explained my position in the post on the reward curve with tempered issuance is:

Excessive incentives for staking, beyond what is necessary for security, can unfortunately over time turn into perverse subsidies, with many downsides.

If you build an application that requires Ethereum to issue more tokens than what is necessary for security, then that application would indeed be negatively affected by adopting MVI. This is very unfortunate. But it cannot be Ethereum's purpose to sustain applications that only are viable under a sub-optimal issuance policy (that impedes its trustlessness). It could be argued that by waiting and waiting, we are just now letting excessive incentives turn into perverse subsidies (with growing special interest groups dependent on cementing these subsidies). 

I certainly do not enjoy doing anything that severely impacts anyone; especially since many people affected by issuance policy are instrumental to Ethereum.
